newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Q2 cocoa grinds to reflect Europe's mixed fortunes.
newsitem.headline: Q2 cocoa grinds to reflect Europe's mixed fortunes.

text.p: Western Europe's second quarter cocoa grind figures, due for release in early July, are likely to produce a mixed picture across the continent but overall volumes could well be down on 1996, analysts said.

The Dutch total, the world's largest, is expected on Friday to move against the overall trend to be slightly up on last year's relatively low total of 90,274 tonnes, with senior traders here saying the country's huge processors are continuing to run at full capacity.
The General Cocoa plant, owned by U.S. giant Cargill, is thought to be processing slightly more beans than last year.

But sources pointed to a switch at Bensdorp Cocoa which changed during 1996 from grinding beans to processing cocoa liquor. This could be the main factor behind just a small rise in the overall Dutch figure, which is thought will not reach the first quarter's 102,338 tonnes.

Analysts said the figures are also likely to show flat demand in much of Europe, although this is somewhat countered by steady growth in offtake in other parts of the world. Second quarter grinds are also seasonally depressed ahead of usually slack chocolate consumption during the summer months.
"It will be up, simply because last year's total was low. Western Europe is one area where demand is pretty weak and any growth we see probably indicates a growth in stocks," said market analyst.
Dutch trade sources described European offtake as steady, but added there had been good growth in South America and to a much lesser extent Asia.
The European market for tablet chocolate was still under pressure and some of the manufacturers in Germany were finding the going tough, they said.

The German grind, difficult to pin down due to capacity shifts, was widely thought to be unchanged to slightly lower than last year's 59,471 tonnes. In the first quarter of this year, it showed an 11.71 percent year-on-year fall to 61,379 tonnes.
The German total will probably be released on July 7 or 8.
"It could be around four percent lower, certainly not more than last year," one trader said.
But in an encouraging sign, German confectionery exports were seen rising further in 1997 due to higher sales to Russia and eastern Europe, export body German Sweets said last week.

In the UK, much depends on the activity of Mars' Selby plant, which most industry sources said had not been active in the second quarter. This would mean the UK total would also be flat at best and could easily be a little lower.
In the second quarter last year the grind was 44,535 tonnes.

But the cool summer so far in Europe may provide a glimmer of hope for some processors in Europe, with traders saying it may spur a pick-up in demand, which will feed through into a strong third quarter total. --Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
